- NEVER run 'python', 'python3', or any interpreter of the source. Only run the executable, and 'node' for your own scratch calculations.
- Use bash. A useful baseline invocation that always succeeds:

- Vary ONLY the argument(s) you are probing; keep the others at safe values so the line you care about is the one that changes.
- Always capture the exit code, and capture stdout and stderr SEPARATELY (e.g. > /tmp/out 2> /tmp/err; echo $?).
- To see raw bytes of output when in doubt, pipe through 'od -c' or 'cat -A'.
- Line 4 echoes the exact raw bytes of --c, so line 4 is your microscope for how Python renders a bytes object.
- Run MANY probes (30+). Be systematic and exhaustive. Report ONLY what you actually observed, with the exact command and exact output. Mark anything you infer but did not directly observe as unverified.


YOUR JOB: adversarial verification. Another agent probed area "argparse-cli" and claims these rules about /workspace/dataset/test20_executable.
Your default assumption is that each rule is WRONG, over-general, or missing an edge case.

For EACH rule below, design and run FRESH commands (do not just repeat their evidence command) that would EXPOSE it if false. Try boundary values, empty values, and combinations. Then judge.

RULES TO ATTACK:
[1] rule: The program name in usage/error text is os.path.basename(sys.argv[0]) — i.e. it comes from argv[0] as invoked, not from the real executable path. For the reference invocation it is exactly 'test20_executable'. A Node reimplementation invoked as 'test20_executable' should hardcode/derive that basename.
    their evidence: Copy of the binary at /tmp/pn/weird-name.bin → `usage: weird-name.bin [-h] ...` / `weird-name.bin: error: ...`. Symlink /tmp/pn/lnk → `usage: lnk [-h] ...`. `bash -c 'exec -a totally_different /workspace/dataset/test20_executable --a 1'` → `usage: totally_different [-h] ...` (proves argv[0], not /proc/self/exe). Relative `./test20_executable` from /workspace/dataset → `usage: test20_executable [-h] ...` (basename only, no './').
[2] rule: The COLUMNS environment variable changes usage-line WRAPPING (argparse uses terminal width minus 2) but never wraps the `{prog}: error: {message}` line. With COLUMNS unset and stdout/stderr not a TTY the width is 80, so the 71-char usage line is emitted on one line. A reimplementation that ignores COLUMNS matches the default harness case.
    their evidence: COLUMNS=40 with a missing arg → usage wraps to 4 lines: `usage: test20_executable [-h] --a A` / `                         --b B --c C` / `                         --d D --e E` / `                         --f F --g G`, then the single unwrapped error line. COLUMNS=1 → one token per line with a 7-space continuation indent. COLUMNS=200 and `env -u COLUMNS` → single 71-char usage line.
[3] rule: argv bytes are decoded as UTF-8 with surrogateescape. Invalid UTF-8 in --a/--c passes the parser cleanly, then the program crashes at .encode() with RC=1 and a traceback on stderr. Invalid UTF-8 in --f is reported by the parser with the lone surrogate rendered as \udcXX. Locale (LC_ALL=C) does not change argv decoding.
    their evidence: --a $'\xff' → RC=1, stderr: `Traceback (most recent call last):` / `  File "test20.py", line 15, in <module>` / `UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode character '\udcff' in position 0: surrogates not allowed` / `[PYI-12659:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test20' due to unhandled exception!`. --c $'A\xffB' → same but `line 17` and `position 1`. --f $'\xff5' → RC=2 `test20_executable: error: argument --f: invalid int value: '\udcff5'` (od confirms literal backslash-u-d-c-f-f). LC_ALL=C with --a 'héllo' --c 'é' → RC=0, stdout diff SAME as default locale.
[4] rule: There is no --version or any option other than -h/--help and --a..--g. Successful runs exit 0 with 12 stdout lines and empty stderr; help exits 0; all parse errors exit 2 with empty stdout.
    their evidence: `--version` alone → RC=2 `...the following arguments are required: --a, --b, --c, --d, --e, --f, --g` (so --version is not an option and was left as an extra). `... --g 2 --version` → `...unrecognized arguments: --version`.

content.text: I ran ~90 fresh invocations. Verdicts below.

verdicts.rule: The program name in usage/error text is os.path.basename(sys.argv[0]) — from argv[0] as invoked, not the real executable path; for the reference invocation it is exactly 'test20_executable'.
verdicts.counterexample: NOT a refutation — fresh probes all agreed, and they pin down exact basename() semantics a Node reimpl must match. `bash -c 'exec -a "$1" /workspace/dataset/test20_executable' _ ""` -> `usage: [-h] --a A ...` / `: error: ...` (empty prog). exec -a '/' , 'a/b/c/' , 'dir/' , './x/' all -> empty prog (trailing slash => basename ''), i.e. NO path normalization first ('/a/b/../c/prog' via node spawnSync argv0 -> `usage: prog [-h] ...`). exec -a 'dir\sub\prog.exe' -> `usage: dir\sub\prog.exe [-h] ...` (backslash is NOT a separator). exec -a '  spaced name  ' -> prog keeps leading/trailing spaces in both usage and error line. exec -a $'AA\nBB' -> prog contains a literal newline, so the usage block spans an extra line. exec -a '-h' / '--a' -> prog is '-h'/'--a' and is NOT parsed as an option. exec -a 'ünïcødé' -> raw UTF-8 bytes on stderr. Copy /tmp/pn2/RENAMED -> 'RENAMED'; symlink /tmp/pn2/sym-link-name -> 'sym-link-name'; PATH=/workspace/dataset test20_executable -> 'test20_executable'; ./dataset/test20_executable and ../dataset/test20_executable -> 'test20_executable' (dir stripped); node spawnSync(argv0:'NODEARGV0') -> 'NODEARGV0'. Same prog string is used in `-h` output (exec -a HELPNAME ... -h -> `usage: HELPNAME [-h] ...`, RC=0, stderr empty). A 68-char prog name forces the usage onto 2 lines even at default width.

verdicts.rule: COLUMNS changes usage-line WRAPPING (argparse uses terminal width minus 2) but never wraps the `{prog}: error: {message}` line. With COLUMNS unset and stdout/stderr not a TTY the width is 80, so the 71-char usage line is emitted on one line. A reimplementation that ignores COLUMNS matches the default harness case.
verdicts.counterexample: Two gaps. (1) COLUMNS also wraps the -h/--help BODY, not just the usage line: `COLUMNS=40 /workspace/dataset/test20_executable -h` -> `  -h, --help  show this help message` / `              and exit`; `COLUMNS=15 ... --help` -> the help text moves to its own lines under `  -h, --help` with a 4-space indent (`    show this` / `    help` / `    message and` / `    exit`). So a reimpl of -h that ignores COLUMNS diverges the moment COLUMNS is set. (2) The '80' is only a fallback for a non-TTY stdout, and the width is read from stdout even though usage goes to stderr: under a pty with `stty cols 40` and COLUMNS unset, usage wraps at 40 even when stderr is redirected to a file (`script -q -c 'stty cols 40; /workspace/dataset/test20_executable 2>/tmp/adv20/pt3err' /dev/null` -> file contains the 4-line wrapped usage). Also COLUMNS=0 / 'abc' / '-5' / '' / '10.5' / '0x40' are ignored as invalid and fall back to the *stdout terminal* size, not to 80: same pty with COLUMNS=0 or COLUMNS=abc still wraps at 40, while in the non-TTY harness they give the 80-width single line. COLUMNS wins over a live tty (pty cols 40 + COLUMNS=100 -> single 71-char line).
verdicts.corrected_rule: argparse's HelpFormatter width = (COLUMNS if it parses as an int > 0 else terminal width of sys.__stdout__ else 80) - 2, and it wraps BOTH the usage line and the -h help body (option-help column + max_help_position), but NEVER the `{prog}: error: {message}` line. Exact boundary for prog 'test20_executable' (usage line = 71 chars): COLUMNS>=73 -> one line; COLUMNS<=72 -> wrapped with a 25-space continuation indent (= len('usage: ')+len(prog)+1); COLUMNS<=13 all collapse to the same one-token-per-line form with a 7-space indent (min text width clamps at 11) — COLUMNS=1,2,9,11,12,13 produced byte-identical output. Leading/trailing spaces and leading '+'/'0' are accepted by int() (' 40 ', '+40', '040' all wrap like 40). The error line stays on one line at every width: verified at COLUMNS=20 with a 152-char 'unrecognized arguments: ...' message, COLUMNS=5 with a 76-char invalid-int value, and COLUMNS=10 with a 76-char prog name. LINES has no effect. A reimpl that ignores COLUMNS matches only when stdout is not a TTY and COLUMNS is unset/invalid.

verdicts.rule: argv bytes are decoded as UTF-8 with surrogateescape; invalid UTF-8 in --a/--c passes the parser then crashes at .encode() with RC=1 + traceback; invalid UTF-8 in --f is reported by the parser with the lone surrogate rendered as \udcXX; locale (LC_ALL=C) does not change argv decoding.
verdicts.counterexample: NOT a refutation — I could not break it, and the locale claim is actually stronger than stated: LC_ALL=C, LC_ALL=POSIX, LC_ALL=C.utf8, LANG=C, PYTHONCOERCECLOCALE=0, PYTHONUTF8=0, PYTHONUTF8=0+PYTHONCOERCECLOCALE=0, PYTHONIOENCODING=ascii and PYTHONIOENCODING=latin-1 ALL produced byte-identical stdout for `--a 'héllo' --c 'é'` (line 4 = b'\xc3\xa9', RC=0) and byte-identical stderr for `--f 'é'` (raw UTF-8 bytes 303 251 inside the quotes, NOT escaped), i.e. the frozen binary ignores PYTHON* io/locale env vars entirely. Fresh invalid-UTF-8 probes: --a $'\xff' -> RC=1, `File "test20.py", line 15` , `'\udcff' in position 0`; --a $'\xc3' (truncated) -> line 15, '\udcc3' position 0; --d $'\xfe' -> line 21, '\udcfe' position 0; --c $'A\xffB' -> line 17, position 1; --c $'AB\xff' -> line 17, position 2. Parser-side: --f $'\xff5' -> RC=2 `invalid int value: '\udcff5'` (od: literal backslash-u-d-c-f-f), --f $'5\xff' -> `'5\udcff'`, --g $'\xff' -> `argument --g: ... '\udcff'`, and LC_ALL=C gives identical bytes. Three additions a stderr-exact reimpl needs: (a) a MULTI-byte invalid run produces the plural form with no character shown — --a $'\xc0\x80' -> `UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode characters in position 0-1: surrogates not allowed`, --a $'\xed\xa0\x80' -> `... position 0-2 ...`, and --f $'\xc0\x80' -> `invalid int value: '\udcc0\udc80'`; (b) --b/--e do NOT crash at .encode() but inside base58 — --b $'\xff' -> line 16 + `base58/__init__.py", line 118, in b58decode` + `line 30, in scrub_input` + `UnicodeEncodeError: 'ascii' codec can't encode character '\udcff' in position 0: ordinal not in range(128)`, and plain non-ASCII (--b 'é') fails the same way with '\xe9'; (c) the `[PYI-NNNNN:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test20' due to unhandled exception!` trailer embeds the PID and is NOT reproducible (I observed PYI-88067, 88073, 88089, 88101, 88122, 88132, 88148, 88154 across runs vs their PYI-12659). Valid 4-byte UTF-8 (--a $'\xf0\x9f\x98\x80') is fine: RC=0, b'79jdou'.

verdicts.rule: There is no --version or any option other than -h/--help and --a..--g. Successful runs exit 0 with 12 stdout lines and empty stderr; help exits 0; all parse errors exit 2 with empty stdout.
verdicts.counterexample: Three independent counterexamples. (1) argparse's allow_abbrev makes prefixes of --help real, working options: `/workspace/dataset/test20_executable --h` -> RC=0 and the full 11-line help on stdout, empty stderr; same for `--he` and `--hel`. Short-option clustering also triggers help: `-hx` -> RC=0 + help, `-habc` -> RC=0 + help. A Node reimpl accepting only -h/--help would emit an error for all five. (2) 'help exits 0' is false when an explicit value is attached: `--help=x` -> RC=2, stderr `test20_executable: error: argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument 'x'`; identical for `--h=x` and `-h=x` (note `-hx` succeeds but `-h=x` fails). (3) 'help exits 0' is also false when an earlier token errors first, because -h only fires when reached: `--f abc -h` -> RC=2 `argument --f: invalid int value: 'abc'`, no help; whereas `-h --f abc`, `--zz -h` and `--a 1 -h --f abc` -> RC=0 + help. Bonus edge cases on 'successful runs exit 0 with 12 stdout lines and empty stderr': `... >/dev/full` -> RC=0 but stdout empty and stderr carries `OSError: [Errno 28] No space left on device` + `Exception ignored in: <_io.TextIOWrapper name='<stdout>' mode='w' encoding='utf-8'>`; `... >&-` -> RC=0 with stderr `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'flush'` (traceback file is `"<string>", line 1`). And there is a fourth outcome besides 0/2: `--f -1 --a 1 --b 2 --c 3 --d 4 --e 5 --g 2` never terminates (timeout 5 -> RC=124, zero bytes on both streams) because b58encode_int loops forever on negatives.
verdicts.corrected_rule: Accepted option spellings are --a..--g (exact, single-letter, so not abbreviable — `--ff 1` and `-a 1` are rejected) plus the help action reachable as -h, --h, --he, --hel, --help, or any -h<chars> cluster (-hx, -habc); matching is case-sensitive (--HELP, --He, --hx are NOT help). No --version/-V and no fromfile (@file) support. Both `--x V` and `--x=V` forms work, later duplicates win (`--a 1 --a 9` uses '9'), and empty values are legal (`--a '' ...` -> line 1 is b''). Outcomes: (a) RC=0 with exactly 12 stdout lines and empty stderr for a normal successful run — always exactly 12 even when values contain newlines/tabs, since print() emits bytes reprs (--c $'a\nb\tc' -> line 4 = b'a\nb\tc'); (b) RC=0 with 11 lines of help on stdout and empty stderr when a help spelling is reached before any error and has no '=' attached; (c) RC=2 with EMPTY stdout and exactly `usage: ...` + `{prog}: error: {msg}` on stderr for every parse error (verified ~20 ways: missing args, invalid int, `--a --b` -> 'expected one argument', 'ignored explicit argument', unrecognized args, positional/`--` leftovers); (d) RC=1 with a traceback for post-parse crashes; (e) non-termination for negative --f/--g. Ordering detail behind their --version evidence: unknown tokens are reported as `unrecognized arguments: ...` ONLY if all seven required options were supplied; otherwise the `the following arguments are required: ...` error wins and the unknown token is never mentioned (`--hx`, `-V`-first, `@somefile`, `-a 1 --b 2 ...` all produced the 'required' error).
